metadata.title: The Broken Ray Transform on the Square

nodes.name: Novikov's reconstruction formula for the attenuated ray transform
nodes.statement: In \cite{novikov, novikov2}, Novikov presents an explicit reconstruction formula for the attenuated ray transform in $2$ dimensions and derives specific conditions for the range in terms of certain integral relations.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit inversion formula and range conditions for the 2D attenuated ray transform.
assumptions: the attenuated ray transform in $2$ dimensions
conclusions: an explicit reconstruction formula
specific conditions for the range in terms of certain integral relations

nodes.name: Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann theorem for X-ray transforms over generic families of curves
nodes.statement: Frigyik, Stefanov, and Uhlmann showed injectivity and stability for the X-ray transform over generic families of curves on smooth manifolds in \cite{xraygeneric} where the attenuation is close to real analytic.
assumptions: generic families of curves on smooth manifolds
the attenuation is close to real analytic
conclusions: injectivity and stability for the X-ray transform

nodes.name: Stefanov-Uhlmann normal operator for the geodesic X-ray transform on simple manifolds
nodes.statement: Previously, Stefanov and Uhlmann in \cite{xraytensor} analyzed the linearized boundary rigidity problem which leads to the geodesic X-ray transform of symmetric 2-tensor fields. They showed in particular that the corresponding normal operator is a pseudodifferential operator of order $-1$ if the manifold is simple.
nodes.statement_short: For simple manifolds the normal operator of the geodesic X-ray transform on 2-tensors is a $\Psi$DO of order $-1$.
assumptions: the manifold is simple
conclusions: the corresponding normal operator is a pseudodifferential operator of order $-1$

nodes.name: Unattenuated Euclidean X-ray transform
nodes.statement: Recall the unattenuated Euclidean X-ray transform of an unknown function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega)$ supported on some bounded domain $\Omega$, which is given by \begin{equation*} Xf(x,\theta) = \int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x+t\theta)\,dt, \quad (x,\theta) \in \Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}. \end{equation*}
nodes.genus: unknown function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega)$ supported on some bounded domain $\Omega$

nodes.name: Conormal spanning condition for injectivity of the X-ray transform
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, the main condition needed for injectivity of $X$ is that the union of the conormal bundles over all available lines must span the cotangent space of the domain (see \cite{xraygeneric}). In the case of the geodesic X-ray transform, this condition holds if all geodesics have no conjugate points, which in turn is true if one assumes that the underlying manifold is simple. But of course such a condition trivially holds for lines in the Euclidean setting.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity needs the conormals of the available lines to span the cotangent space; automatic in the Euclidean case.
assumptions: the union of the conormal bundles over all available lines must span the cotangent space of the domain
conclusions: the main condition needed for injectivity of $X$

nodes.name: Empty analytic wavefront set forces a compactly supported function to vanish
nodes.statement: For if an unknown function $f$ supported in $\Omega$ satisfies $WF_{A}(f) \cap T^{*}\Omega = \emptyset$, then $f$ must be entire and compactly supported, and hence must vanish identically.
nodes.statement_short: If $WF_A(f)$ misses $T^*\Omega$ then $f$ is entire and compactly supported, hence $f \equiv 0$.
assumptions: an unknown function $f$ supported in $\Omega$ satisfies $WF_{A}(f) \cap T^{*}\Omega = \emptyset$
conclusions: $f$ must be entire and compactly supported, and hence must vanish identically

nodes.name: Broken ray transform uniqueness problem
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, if $(\Omega, g)$ is a compact Riemannian manifold with appropriate conditions, and $E \subset \partial \Omega$ is open, the question is the following: do the integrals of an unknown function $f$ along all broken rays starting and ending on $E$, and which reflect only on $\partial \Omega \setminus E$, uniquely determine $f$?
nodes.statement_short: Do integrals of $f$ over all broken rays with endpoints in $E$, reflecting only on $\partial\Omega \setminus E$, determine $f$?

nodes.name: Reflection tomography for non-Euclidean metrics
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, reflection tomography of this nature for non-Euclidean metrics has not yet been treated in general.

nodes.name: Obstruction to the generic-curve technique after reflection
nodes.statement: The technique of \cite{xraygeneric} relies on constructing local coordinates about some fixed geodesic $\gamma_{0}$ in order to show that the normal operator has nice microlocal properties. But, if one were to reflect from the boundary the family of geodesics associated with such coordinates, one no longer has local coordinates around the corresponding reflected segment of $\gamma_{0}$. As such, we will focus just on the Euclidean case, and in particular we will consider the unit square in $\rn{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reflecting a family of geodesics destroys the local coordinates that the generic-curve method needs, so the paper restricts to the Euclidean square.

nodes.name: Generalizability to convex domains with piecewise flat reflective boundaries
nodes.statement: It is the author's belief, however, that the results herein are generalizable to at least to convex domains in $\rn{n}$ with piecewise flat reflective boundaries.
assumptions: convex domains in $\rn{n}$ with piecewise flat reflective boundaries
conclusions: the results herein are generalizable

nodes.name: Eskin's uniqueness result for broken rays reflecting off convex obstacles
nodes.statement: In particular, Eskin proved a uniqueness result for $C^{\infty}$ unknown functions in $2$-dimensions given knowledge of broken rays that reflect off of known convex obstacles in the domain's interior (\cite{eskin}). There the weight function is taken to be a smooth electric potential $V(x)$.
assumptions: $C^{\infty}$ unknown functions in $2$-dimensions
knowledge of broken rays that reflect off of known convex obstacles in the domain's interior
conclusions: a uniqueness result

nodes.name: Ilmavirta's injectivity result on the disk
nodes.statement: Furthermore, the recent work of Ilmavirta in \cite{joonas} proves an injectivity result on the disk for open subsets $E$ of the boundary when the unknown function $f$ is uniformly quasianalytic in the angular variable (when written in polar coordinates).
assumptions: open subsets $E$ of the boundary
the unknown function $f$ is uniformly quasianalytic in the angular variable (when written in polar coordinates)
conclusions: an injectivity result on the disk

nodes.name: Calderon problem with partial Cauchy data
nodes.statement: In short, they consider the problem of recovering an unknown potential $q \in L^{\infty}(\Omega)$ given the partial Cauchy data set

nodes.name: Partial Cauchy data set $\mathcal{C}_{q}^{\Gamma_{D}, \Gamma_{N}}$
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \mathcal{C}_{q}^{\Gamma_{D}, \Gamma_{N}} & = \{ (u \vert_{\Gamma_{D}}, \partial_{\nu}u \vert_{\Gamma_{N}}) \, | \, (-\Delta + q)u = 0 \mathrm{ in }\Omega,\, u \in H_{\Delta}(\Omega),\\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \mathrm{supp}(u \vert_{\partial \Omega}) \subset \Gamma_{D} \}. \end{align*} Here $H_{\Delta}(\Omega) = \{ u \in L^{2}(\Omega) \, | \, \Delta u \in L^{2}(\Omega)\}$ and $\Gamma_{D}, \Gamma_{N}$ are two (possibly very small) open subsets of $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Salo-Kenig broken ray identity from partial Cauchy data
nodes.statement: The authors of \cite{salokenig} then prove the following: let $\Gamma_{i} \subset \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}}$ such that there exists a nonempty open subset $E$ of $\partial M_{0}$, and suppose $\Gamma_{D} = \Gamma_{N} = \Gamma$ for some neighborhood $\Gamma$ in $\partial M$ of the set $\overline{\partial M_{+} \cup \partial M_{-} \cup \Gamma_{a}}$ for $\Gamma_{a} = \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}} \setminus \Gamma_{i}$. If $q_{1},q_{2}$ are two potentials such that $\mathcal{C}_{g,q_{1}}^{\Gamma_{D},\Gamma_{N}} = \mathcal{C}_{g,q_{2}}^{\Gamma_{D},\Gamma_{N}}$, then \begin{equation*} \int_{0}^{L}e^{-2\lambda t}( c(q_{1} - q_{2})\,{\hat{}}\,(2\lambda, \gamma(t))\,dt = 0 \end{equation*} for all nontangential broken rays $\gamma: [0,L] \to M_{0}$ with endpoints in $E$ and for any $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$. Here $( \cdot )\,{\hat{}}$ denotes the Fourier transform with respect to $x_{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal partial Cauchy data forces the attenuated broken ray transform of $c(q_1-q_2)^{\hat{}}$ to vanish on all nontangential broken rays with endpoints in $E$.
assumptions: let $\Gamma_{i} \subset \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}}$ such that there exists a nonempty open subset $E$ of $\partial M_{0}$

suppose $\Gamma_{D} = \Gamma_{N} = \Gamma$ for some neighborhood $\Gamma$ in $\partial M$ of the set $\overline{\partial M_{+} \cup \partial M_{-} \cup \Gamma_{a}}$ for $\Gamma_{a} = \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}} \setminus \Gamma_{i}$
If $q_{1},q_{2}$ are two potentials such that $\mathcal{C}_{g,q_{1}}^{\Gamma_{D},\Gamma_{N}} = \mathcal{C}_{g,q_{2}}^{\Gamma_{D},\Gamma_{N}}$
conclusions: for all nontangential broken rays $\gamma: [0,L] \to M_{0}$ with endpoints in $E$ and for any $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$

nodes.name: Unifying partial data results for the Calderon problem
nodes.statement: Thus, the unique determination of the potential from such partial data could be resolved if one can show injectivity of the broken ray transform considered here. Ultimately, the big hope is that the collection of currently existing partial data results for the Calder\'on problem can be more unified, perhaps by using this (or some other) new approach to the problem.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of this broken ray transform would settle unique determination from partial Cauchy data and might unify partial-data results.

nodes.name: Setup domain: general smooth domain for definitions, square for the theorems
nodes.statement: We will state the problem setup and definition in the case of a general domain $\Omega$ with smooth boundary. However, the main theorems themselves assume further that $\Omega$ is the square.

nodes.name: Outgoing and ingoing unit vector sets $\Gamma_{\pm}$ and $\Gamma_{\pm}(E)$
nodes.statement:
Let $\Omega$ be a smooth bounded domain in $n{n}$ and define $\Gamma_{\pm} = \{(x,	heta) \in \partial \Omega 	imes \mathbb{S}^{n-1} \, | \, \pm 
u(x) \cdot 	heta >0\}$ as the set of outgoing and ingoing unit vectors on $\partial \Omega$, respectively. Here $
u(x)$ is the outward unit normal vector to $\partial \Omega$. We also define, for a general open subset $E \subset \partial \Omega$, the set  egin{equation} \Gamma_{\pm}(E) := \{(x,	heta) \in S\Omega \, | \, x \in E, \pm 	heta \cdot 
u(x) > 0\}. \end{equation}
nodes.genus: the set of outgoing and ingoing unit vectors on $\partial \Omega$

nodes.name: Attenuation $\sigma$ smooth and vanishing near the boundary
nodes.statement: Assume that $\sigma \in C^{\infty}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$ and vanishes near $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Regular broken ray
nodes.statement: We will call any unit speed curve $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ a \textit{regular broken ray} in $\Omega$ if \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] its associated tangent vector field $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(t), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(t))$ intersects $\Gamma_{-}(E)$\\ \item[(b)] it consists of finitely many straight line segments $\gamma_{x,\theta,1}, \gamma_{x,\theta,2}, \ldots, \gamma_{x,\theta,N}$ before hitting $E$ again\\ \item[(c)] it does not intersect $\partial E$, and\\ \item[(d)] it obeys the geometrical optics reflection law \begin{equation} \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j+1}(0) = \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j}) - 2\left\langle \nu(\gamma_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j})),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j}) \right\rangle \nu(\gamma_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j})), \,1 \leq j \leq N. \end{equation} \end{enumerate} Here $L_{j}$ denotes the length of $\gamma_{x,\theta,j}$ and the subscripts refer to the fact that $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(0), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(0)) = (x,\theta)$.
nodes.statement_short: A unit speed curve that enters through $E$, consists of finitely many segments obeying the optical reflection law, and avoids $\partial E$.
differentia: its associated tangent vector field $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(t), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(t))$ intersects $\Gamma_{-}(E)$
it consists of finitely many straight line segments $\gamma_{x,\theta,1}, \gamma_{x,\theta,2}, \ldots, \gamma_{x,\theta,N}$ before hitting $E$ again
it obeys the geometrical optics reflection law

nodes.name: Billiard map $T$, projections, travel times and reflection count $N(x,\theta)$
nodes.statement: We use the notation $T:\Gamma_{-} \to \Gamma_{-}$ to denote the billiard map mapping a vector $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}$ to $(x',\theta') \in \Gamma_{-}$, where $x'$ is the intersection point of the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ with $\partial \Omega$, and $\theta'$ is the reflected direction. We use the maps $\pi_{1},\pi_{2}$ to denote the projections $\Gamma_{-} \to \partial \Omega$ and $\Gamma_{-} \to \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, respectively. Also $\tau_{\pm}(x,\theta) = \min \{ t \geq 0 \, | \, x + t\theta \in \partial \Omega\}$ are the positive and negative travel times from a given unit tangent vector $(x,\theta) \in S\Omega$, and $N(x,\theta)$ for $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ will denote the number of reflections of the given trajectory before intersecting $E$. We use the notation $g^{\#}(x,\theta) := g(x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta, \theta)$ to denote the extension of a function $g$ on $\Gamma_{-}$ to $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation: billiard map $T$ on $\Gamma_-$, projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$, travel times $\tau_\pm$, reflection count $N$, and the extension $g^{\#}$.
nodes.genus: the billiard map mapping a vector $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}$ to $(x',\theta') \in \Gamma_{-}$
differentia: $x'$ is the intersection point of the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ with $\partial \Omega$

nodes.name: Unattenuated broken ray transform $I_{0,E}$
nodes.statement: First we consider the unattenuated broken ray transform $I_{0,E}$ with respect to the accessible set $E$, so as not to be distracted by technicalities. The operator $I_{0,E}:L^{2}(\Omega) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$, where $d\Sigma = |\nu(x) \cdot \theta|\, dS(x)\, d\theta$ is the standard measure on $\Gamma_{-}$, is defined by \begin{equation} I_{0, E}f(\gamma_{x,\theta}) = I_{0, E}f(x,\theta) := \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} f(\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \end{equation} for all regular broken rays $\gamma_{x,\theta}$. Here \begin{equation} (z_{j}(x,\theta),\theta_{j}(x,\theta)) = T^{j}(x+\tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta,\theta), \quad (x,\theta) \in S\Omega.
nodes.statement_short: Sum over reflections of the line integrals of $f$ along the segments of the broken ray leaving $(x,\theta)$.
differentia: I_{0, E}f(\gamma_{x,\theta}) = I_{0, E}f(x,\theta) := \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} f(\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt.

nodes.name: $I_{0,E}$ is not expected to be bounded
nodes.statement: Since in general there may be regular broken rays in $\Omega$ with arbitrarily many reflections, we cannot expect for $I_{0,E}:L^{2}(\Omega) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ to be a bounded operator.
nodes.statement_short: Arbitrarily many reflections prevent boundedness of $I_{0,E}$ on $L^2$.
assumptions: in general there may be regular broken rays in $\Omega$ with arbitrarily many reflections
conclusions: we cannot expect for $I_{0,E}:L^{2}(\Omega) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ to be a bounded operator

nodes.name: Cutoff operator $\alpha I_{0,E}$
nodes.statement: Thus, we will instead consider the cutoff operator $\alpha I_{0, E}$, where $\alpha:\Gamma_{-}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth cutoff function supported on some subset of broken rays that have at most $N_{max} \geq 0$ reflections. The boundedness of this cutoff operator, with possible attenuation, will be proved later when we introduce the more general weighted transform.
differentia: supported on some subset of broken rays that have at most $N_{max} \geq 0$ reflections

nodes.name: Corner reflections on polyhedral domains and on the square
nodes.statement: Although general polyhedral domains lack obvious reflection rules at the corners (some authors ignore such trajectories and some define them in terms of limits of regular trajectories, e.g. \cite{eskin}), the special symmetrical nature of the square does give an unambiguous rule for such reflections. But one still runs into the problem that the composite functions $z_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta)$ are not real analytic for $(x,\theta)$ associated with a corner point. One simple, albeit more restrictive route, is to assume that the subset $E$ also includes a small neighborhood of each corner. In that case, all broken rays with corner points are just ballistic X-rays. More generally, one can cut out the rays with corner points from the measurement operator. However, if one assumes the attenuation coefficient to vanish in a neighborhood of the boundary, it is still possible to treat rays with corners as we will discuss later.
nodes.statement_short: The square has an unambiguous corner reflection rule, but $z_j,\theta_j$ fail to be real analytic at corners; several remedies are possible.

nodes.name: $N(x,\theta)$ is piecewise constant and its discontinuities come from reflections on $\partial E$
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $N(x,\theta)$ is piecewise constant, which leads to the unfortunate fact that $I_{0, E}$ in general does not preserve the smoothness of a function. Since we are considering a convex domain (flat) in this work, the discontinuities of $N(x,\theta)$ occur only for $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ such that $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ has a reflection occurring at some point in $\partial E$.
nodes.statement_short: $N$ is piecewise constant, so $I_{0,E}$ need not preserve smoothness; jumps occur exactly for rays reflecting on $\partial E$.
assumptions: we are considering a convex domain (flat) in this work
conclusions: $N(x,\theta)$ is piecewise constant
$I_{0, E}$ in general does not preserve the smoothness of a function
the discontinuities of $N(x,\theta)$ occur only for $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ such that $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ has a reflection occurring at some point in $\partial E$

nodes.name: Localization by smooth cutoffs $\alpha_{k}$ and detection of covectors
nodes.statement: This is the reason they are not classified as \textit{regular} broken rays. To eliminate such discontinuities introduced by $N(x,\theta)$ we will use a collection of smooth cutoff functions $\alpha_{k}$ on $\Gamma_{-}(E)$ so as to remove the bad parts of $I_{0, E}$. For example, for each point $(x_{0},\theta_{0}) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ where $N(x,\theta)$ is continuous (i.e. $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ and nearby rays do not touch corner points), we may multiply $I_{\sigma, E}$ by a smooth function $\alpha(x,\theta) \equiv 1$ near $(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$ and such that $N(x,\theta) \vert_{\mathrm{supp}(\alpha)}$ is constant. This localized operator will have a constant number of reflections and thus behaves very much like the usual generalized ray transform, which makes it possible to apply the microlocal analytic techniques of \cite{xraygeneric}. Of course, additional care is needed to deal with broken rays that contain corner points, which we discuss later. The central idea is that for fixed $(x,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega \setminus 0$, any broken ray $\gamma$ passing through $x$ with direction normal to $\xi$ will allow for the detection of $(x,\xi)$ in $\mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying by cutoffs with locally constant $N$ makes the operator behave like a generalized ray transform, so covectors conormal to a broken ray can be detected.

nodes.name: Analytic wavefront set notation $\mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$
nodes.statement: From hereon we use the notation $\mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$ to denote the analytic wavefront set of $f$.

nodes.name: Path unfolding
nodes.statement: The main idea we use in order to apply microlocal analytic techniques to the operator is a well-known method of billiards called path unfolding. Essentially, we can unfold any broken ray in $\Omega$ into a straight line on a different domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ defined by reflecting $\Omega$ across each of its edges repeatedly to obtain a tiling of $\rn{2}$. Similarly, we can extend $f$ to a function $\widetilde{f}$ on $\widetilde{\Omega}$ by reflection across $\partial \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold a broken ray into a straight line by repeatedly reflecting $\Omega$ across its edges to tile $\rn{2}$, extending $f$ to $\widetilde{f}$.
differentia: we can unfold any broken ray in $\Omega$ into a straight line on a different domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ defined by reflecting $\Omega$ across each of its edges repeatedly to obtain a tiling of $\rn{2}$
we can extend $f$ to a function $\widetilde{f}$ on $\widetilde{\Omega}$ by reflection across $\partial \Omega$

nodes.name: Reflection signature
nodes.statement: We will use indices $(l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ to denote how many horizontal and vertical reflections a given broken ray undergoes on the unfolded domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ before returning to the set $E$. We call this the \textit{reflection signature} of a path. For example, $(-1,2)$ indicates $1$ reflection to the left and $2$ reflections upwards.
differentia: denote how many horizontal and vertical reflections a given broken ray undergoes on the unfolded domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ before returning to the set $E$

nodes.name: Point reflection maps $R_{l_{1},l_{2}}$ and inverses
nodes.statement: The following transformations and their respective inverses will be useful when translating between vectors on $T\Omega$ and $T \widetilde{\Omega}$. Given a reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$, we can compute the reflected version of a point $w \in \Omega$ by \begin{align} \widetilde{w} = R_{l_{1},l_{2}}(w) & = \left( l_{1} + \frac{1 - (-1)^{l_{1}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{1}}w_{1}, l_{2} + \frac{1 - (-1)^{l_{2}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{2}}w_{2} \right)\\ w = R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\widetilde{w}) & = \left( (-1)^{l_{1}+1}l_{1} + \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{1}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{1}}\widetilde{w}_{1}, \, (-1)^{l_{2}+1}l_{2} + \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{2}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{2}}\widetilde{w}_{2} \right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit affine formulas mapping a point $w \in \Omega$ to its copy $\widetilde{w}$ under the $(l_1,l_2)$ reflection, and back.
nodes.genus: the reflected version of a point $w \in \Omega$

nodes.name: Angle reflection maps $S_{l_{1},l_{2}}$ and inverses
nodes.statement: Similarly, given an angle $\theta$, $S_{l_{1},l_{2}}(\theta)$ is the angle after an $(l_{1},l_{2})$ reflection. \begin{align} \eta = S_{l_{1},l_{2}}(\theta) &= (-1)^{l_{1}+l_{2}}\theta + \frac{\pi}{2}\left[ 1 - (-1)^{l_{1}} \right]\\ \theta = S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\eta) & = (-1)^{l_{2}}\left( (-1)^{l_{1}} \eta + \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{1}}}{2}\pi \right). \end{align}

nodes.name: Reflected extension $\widetilde{f}$
nodes.statement: Such formulas can be verified with straightforward geometry. Using this notation, we have \begin{equation} \widetilde{f}(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} f(R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(x)) & \textrm{ if }x \in [l_{1},l_{1}+1] \times [l_{2},l_{2}+1]\\ & (l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}, \end{array}\right. \end{equation} which obviously makes sense even for compactly supported distributions in $\Omega$.

nodes.name: Unfolded (X-ray-like) form of $I_{0,E}f$
nodes.statement: Note that one can also write $I_{0,E}f$ in the form \begin{equation} I_{0, E}f(x,\theta) = \int_{0}^{L(\gamma_{x,\theta})}\widetilde{f}(x+t\theta)\,dt, \end{equation} which resembles the usual X-ray transform.
nodes.statement_short: $I_{0,E}f$ equals the straight-line integral of the unfolded function $\widetilde{f}$.

nodes.name: Cutoff $\alpha$ localizing broken rays of a fixed reflection signature
nodes.statement: In particular, let $\alpha(x,\theta)$ be a smooth cutoff function on $\Gamma_{-}$ that localizes around some neighborhood of broken rays with the same reflection signature. Because $\widetilde{f}$ vanishes outside of the extended domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$, we may assume all broken rays in the support of $\alpha$ have the same length $L$, by extending them outside if necessary. Note that such rays may contain a corner point. We can then make sense of $\alpha I_{0,E}f$ where $f$ is a distribution.
nodes.statement_short: A smooth cutoff supported on rays of one reflection signature, all extendable to a common length $L$, makes $\alpha I_{0,E}f$ meaningful for distributions.
differentia: localizes around some neighborhood of broken rays with the same reflection signature
all broken rays in the support of $\alpha$ have the same length $L$, by extending them outside if necessary

nodes.name: Distributional pairing for $\alpha I_{0,E}f$
nodes.statement: Specifically, if $f \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\phi \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\rn{2})$ we have \begin{align*} \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \alpha(x,\theta)I_{0,E}f(x,\theta)\phi(x,\theta)\,d\Sigma & = \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\alpha(x,\theta) \left( \int_{0}^{L}\widetilde{f}(x + t\theta)\,dt \right) \phi(x,\theta)\,d\Sigma\\ & = \int_{\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}}\alpha^{\#}(z,\theta) \phi^{\#}(z,\theta)\widetilde{f}(z) \,dz\,d\theta. \end{align*} Thus, \begin{equation} \langle \alpha I_{0,E}f, \phi \rangle = \left\langle \widetilde{f}, \int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\alpha^{\#}(\cdot, \theta)\phi^{\#}(\cdot, \theta)\,d\theta \right \rangle, \end{equation} which is well defined for $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\Omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: Duality computation showing $\langle \alpha I_{0,E}f, \phi\rangle$ pairs $\widetilde{f}$ against $\int_{\mathbb{S}^1}\alpha^{\#}\phi^{\#}d\theta$.

nodes.name: Visible set $\mathcal{M}$
nodes.statement: For a given $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$, we define the \textit{visible set} by \begin{align} \mathcal{M} & := \{x \in \Omega \, | \, \forall \xi \in \mathbb{S}^{1}, (x,\xi) \in N^{*}\gamma \textrm{ for some regular broken ray $\gamma$}\\ & \hspace{7cm} \textrm{ with $N(\gamma) \leq N_{max}$}\}. \notag \end{align}
differentia: \forall \xi \in \mathbb{S}^{1}, (x,\xi) \in N^{*}\gamma \textrm{ for some regular broken ray $\gamma$}

nodes.name: Visible set for two adjacent edges of the square
nodes.statement: One simple example of what $\mathcal{M}$ looks like is the case when $E$ contains two adjacent edges of the square $\Omega = (0,1)^2$. Then $\mathcal{M} = \Omega$.

nodes.name: Visible set for a hemisphere of the ball
nodes.statement: Similarly, if $\Omega = \{x \in \rn{n} \, | \, |x| \leq 1 \}$, then for $E$ containing a hemisphere we have $\mathcal{M} = \Omega$.

nodes.name: Convex hulls of the components of $E$ lie in $\mathcal{M}$
nodes.statement: In general, if $E = \bigcup_{j}E_{j}$ is a union of connected open subsets $E_{j}$ of the boundary, then we always have $\bigcup_{j} \mathrm{ch}(E_{j})\subset \mathcal{M}$, where $\mathrm{ch}$ denotes the closed convex hull. However, this is the part of $\mathcal{M}$ that is attributed to only ballistic (unreflected) X-rays.
nodes.statement_short: For $E = \bigcup_j E_j$ one always has $\bigcup_j \mathrm{ch}(E_j) \subset \mathcal{M}$, coming from ballistic rays only.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (injectivity of $I_{0,E}$ on the square)
nodes.statement: Let $E \subset \partial \Omega$ be open, let $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be the corresponding visible set, and let $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$. Then $I_{0, E}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: On the square, the unattenuated broken ray transform is injective on $L^2(K)$ for $K$ compactly inside the visible set.
assumptions: Let $E \subset \partial \Omega$ be open
let $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$
let $\mathcal{M}$ be the corresponding visible set
let $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$
conclusions: Then $I_{0, E}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$

nodes.name: Attenuated broken ray transform $I_{\sigma,E}$
nodes.statement:
For the moment, consider an attenuation function $\sigma \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega 	imes \mathbb{S}^{1})$ which vanishes near $\partial \Omega$. nodes.name: Weight functions $w_{j}$ on $S\Omega$
nodes.statement: The weight functions $w_{j}$ on $S\Omega$ are given by \begin{align} w_{j}(y,\eta) & = \exp\left( -\sum_{m=0}^{j-1} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\sigma( z_{m-j}+\tau \theta_{m-j},\theta_{m-j})\,d\tau\right) \exp\left( -\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\sigma(y - \tau \eta, \eta)\,d\tau \right)\notag\\ & = \exp\left( -\sum_{m=1}^{j} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\sigma( z_{-m}+\tau \theta_{-m},\theta_{-m})\,d\tau\right) \exp\left( -\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\sigma(y - \tau \eta, \eta)\,d\tau \right)\notag \end{align}

nodes.name: The weight functions $w_{j}$ are smooth
nodes.statement: It is important to note that because $\sigma$ vanishes near $\partial \Omega$, the weight functions $w_{j}$ are smooth. The reason is that we can circumscribe $\Omega$ with the ball $B = B\left( \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)$ and then replace $z_{m-j}(y,\eta) = \pi_{1} \circ T^{m-j}(y+ \tau_{-}(y,\eta)\eta,\eta)$ with the last point of $\partial B$ that intersects the line $z_{m-j}(y,\eta) + t\theta_{m-j}(y,\eta)$ for $t \leq 0$. This point is smoothly dependent on $(y,\eta) \in \Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Because $\sigma$ vanishes near $\partial\Omega$, backward endpoints can be moved to the circumscribed circle $\partial B$, making $w_j$ smooth.
assumptions: because $\sigma$ vanishes near $\partial \Omega$
conclusions: the weight functions $w_{j}$ are smooth

nodes.name: Extended attenuation $\widetilde{\sigma}$ and unfolded weight $\widetilde{w}$
nodes.statement: Just as we could rewrite the unattenuated broken ray transform as a standard X-ray transform for the augmented function $\widetilde{f}$, we can do the same for the attenuated case. First we define an extension of $\sigma$ on $\widetilde{\Omega}\times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ by \begin{equation} \widetilde{\sigma}(x,\theta) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \sigma( R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(x), S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\theta)) & \textrm{ for }x \in [l_{1},l_{1}+1] \times [l_{2},l_{2}+1],\\ & \quad (l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}. \end{array}\right. \end{equation} Then $\widetilde{w}(x,\theta) := \exp\left( -\int_{0}^{L(\gamma_{x,-\theta})}\widetilde{\sigma}(x-\tau\theta,\theta)\,d\tau\right)$ is the associated weight for $(x,\theta) \in \widetilde{\Omega} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$. We've used the notation $L(\gamma_{x,-\theta})$ to mean the length of the half broken ray with initial condition $(x,-\theta)$ before hitting some copy of $E$ in $\widetilde{\Omega}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reflect $\sigma$ across the tiling to get $\widetilde{\sigma}$, and define the unfolded attenuation weight $\widetilde{w}$ by integrating it backwards.

nodes.name: The unfolded attenuation $\widetilde{\sigma}$ is generally not analytic
nodes.statement: Obviously, $\sigma \equiv 0$ implies that $w \equiv 1$, which is analytic. However, for general $\sigma$ that are analytic on $\Omega$, it is not generally true that $\widetilde{\sigma}$ is analytic. In fact, it is easy to see that $\widetilde{\sigma}$ has symmetries somewhat like that of a doubly periodic function, which if analytic would necessarily be constant (the Weierstrass $\wp$-function is doubly periodic but has poles). This is the reason why we start with the case that the weight function is identically $1$ (equivalently $\sigma = 0$) and then prove stability for $C^{2}$ perturbations of $\sigma$ that remain $0$ in a neighborhood of $\partial \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Doubly-periodic-like symmetry of $\widetilde{\sigma}$ blocks analyticity, forcing the strategy: start from $\sigma=0$, then perturb in $C^2$.
assumptions: for general $\sigma$ that are analytic on $\Omega$
conclusions: it is not generally true that $\widetilde{\sigma}$ is analytic

nodes.name: Lemma 1 (boundedness of the cutoff broken ray transform)
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Gamma_{-})$ and suppose all regular broken rays in $\mathrm{supp}(\alpha)$ have $\leq N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$ reflections. Then $I_{\sigma, E}:L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1}) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ is bounded.

suppose all regular broken rays in $\mathrm{supp}(\alpha)$ have $\leq N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$ reflections
conclusions: Then $I_{\sigma, E}:L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1}) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ is bounded

nodes.name: Santalo-type identity on $\Gamma_{-}$
nodes.statement: First we recall an identity from \cite{inversesource} which asserts that for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, we have \begin{equation*} \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrating along inward rays from $\Gamma_-$ against $d\Sigma$ equals integrating over $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.
assumptions: for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$
conclusions: \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First we recall an identity from \cite{inversesource} which asserts that for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, we have \begin{equation*} \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta. \end{equation*} Now observe that \begin{align*} \| \alpha I_{\sigma, E} f(x,\theta) \|_{L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})}^{2} & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} |\alpha(x,\theta)|^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} [w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\ &\leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} \chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}(t)[w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\ & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \|\chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\|[w_{j}f](z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\ & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\Gamma_{-}} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(x+t\theta,\theta)|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})}^{2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Insert the cited Santalo-type identity, then Cauchy-Schwarz each of the $\leq N_{max}+1$ segment integrals and sum.

nodes.name: Recall the phase-space integration identity
nodes.statement: First we recall an identity from \cite{inversesource} which asserts that for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, we have \begin{equation*} \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Quote the identity of the cited work converting $\Gamma_-$ ray integrals into integrals over $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Estimate the norm segment by segment
nodes.statement: Now observe that \begin{align*} \| \alpha I_{\sigma, E} f(x,\theta) \|_{L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})}^{2} & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} |\alpha(x,\theta)|^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} [w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\ &\leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} \chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}(t)[w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\ & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \|\chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\|[w_{j}f](z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\ & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\Gamma_{-}} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(x+t\theta,\theta)|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\ & = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})}^{2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound each segment integral by Cauchy-Schwarz with $\|\chi\|^2 \le \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)$ and sum over $j \le N_{max}$.

nodes.name: Construction of the cutoff functions $\alpha_{k}$ on maximal constant-signature neighborhoods
nodes.statement: To formulate a stability estimate, we must first parametrize a family of regular broken rays, having an upper bound on the number of reflections, and whose conormal bundles cover $T^{*}\Omega$. Fix a positive $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$. For each regular broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with $N(x_{0},\theta_{0}) \leq N_{max}$, let $(l_{1},l_{2})$ be it's reflection signature on $\widetilde{\Omega}$. If $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ has no corner points, then find a maximal connected neighborhood $U \subset \Gamma_{-}(E)$ containing $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ such that all broken rays with initial data in $U$ are regular, have no corner points, and have the same reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$ (See Figure \ref{fig:beam}). In particular, $U$ itself contains no corner points. We then choose a smooth cutoff function $\alpha_{k}$ on $\Gamma_{-}$ that is equal to $1$ on a compact subset of $U$ and vanishes outside of $U$.
nodes.statement_short: For each broken ray without corners take a maximal neighborhood $U$ of regular rays with the same reflection signature and a cutoff $\alpha_k$ supported in $U$.
differentia: equal to $1$ on a compact subset of $U$ and vanishes outside of $U$
all broken rays with initial data in $U$ are regular, have no corner points, and have the same reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$

nodes.name: Cutoff construction when the initial point is a corner
nodes.statement: If $x_{0}$ is a corner point, then we consider all directed lines $\mathcal{L} = \{(x+t\theta,\theta) \, | \, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ for $(x,\theta)$ in some neighborhood of $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ such that $N(x,\theta)$ is constant. Then take the intersection of $\mathcal{L}$ with the ball $B = \left( \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)$ of radius $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ whose boundary $\partial B$ circumscribes $\Omega$. We then define a smooth function $\alpha$ on $\partial B \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ supported in $\partial B \times \mathbb{S}^{1} \cap \mathcal{L}$. We may then extend $\alpha$ to $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ to be constant on all directed lines $(x+t\theta, \theta)$. Its restriction to $\Gamma_{-}(\partial \Omega)$ is the cutoff we seek.
nodes.statement_short: For a corner starting point, build $\alpha$ on $\partial B \times \mathbb{S}^1$ constant along directed lines and restrict it to $\Gamma_-(\partial\Omega)$.
differentia: extend $\alpha$ to $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ to be constant on all directed lines $(x+t\theta, \theta)$

nodes.name: Regularized operator $I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ and normal operator $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\alpha_{k}$ be a sum of smooth cutoff functions on $\Gamma_{-}(E)$ in the sense of the previous paragraph, and consider the regularized operator \begin{equation} I_{\sigma,E,\alpha} := \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\alpha_{k} I_{\sigma,E}. \end{equation} Then \begin{equation} N_{\sigma, E, \alpha} := I_{\sigma, E,\alpha}^{*} I_{\sigma, E, \alpha} = \sum_{k_{1}=1,k_{2}=1}^{N_{\alpha}}I_{\sigma,E}^{*}\alpha_{k_{1}}\alpha_{k_{2}}I_{\sigma, E}. \end{equation} The transpose is taken with respect to the standard measure $|\nu(x) \cdot \theta|\,dS(x)\,d\theta$ on $\Gamma_{-}(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum the localized transforms $\alpha_k I_{\sigma,E}$ and form the normal operator $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = I^*_{\sigma,E,\alpha}I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$.

nodes.name: Cutoff functions $\alpha_{k}$ may be assumed to have disjoint support
nodes.statement: Note that we may as well assume that the $\alpha_{k}$ functions have disjoint support, since it won't change the kind of terms present in the normal operator (if two such cutoff functions $\alpha_{k_{1}}$ and $\alpha_{k_{2}}$ have overlapping support, then their product is also smooth with the supported broken rays localized just as in the previous construction).

nodes.name: Microlocally visible set $\mathcal{M}'$
nodes.statement: We also define the \textit{microlocally visible set} by \begin{equation} \mathcal{M}' := \{ (z,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega \, | \, (z,\xi) \in N^{*}\gamma_{x,\theta} \textrm{ for some }(x,\theta) \textrm{ with }\alpha(x,\theta) > 0\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Why a reflection threshold $N_{max}$ is needed
nodes.statement: One reason we need to impose an upper bound on the number of reflections is that as $N$ increases, the open level sets of $N(x,\theta)$ shrink in measure to zero. Similarly, the neighborhoods in $\Gamma_{-}$ on which we have constant reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$ become infinitesimal as $|l_{1}|+|l_{2}| \to \infty$. Thus $\alpha$ will not be smooth unless we apply some threshold.
nodes.statement_short: Level sets of $N$ and constant-signature neighborhoods shrink to measure zero, so $\alpha$ is smooth only under a threshold.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (stability estimate)
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] Fix $\sigma$ that is $0$ in a neighborhood of $\partial \Omega$, and choose $\alpha \in C^{\infty}(\Gamma_{-})$ as above with reflection threshold $N_{max}$. Fix a set $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$ compactly contained in the visible set $\mathcal{M}$. If $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$, then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{C}\|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq \|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f \|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \leq C\|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}. \end{equation} \item[(b)] Let $\alpha^{0}$ be as above related to some fixed $\sigma_{0}$. Assume that $I_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$. Then estimate (\ref{eq:stabilityestimate}) remains true for $(\sigma, \alpha)$ in a small $C^{2}$ neighborhood of $(\sigma_{0}, \alpha^{0})$ such that $\sigma \equiv 0$ near $\partial \Omega$, and with a uniform constant $C > 0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of $I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ on $L^2(K)$ gives a two-sided $L^2$-$H^1$ stability estimate for $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$, stable under small $C^2$ perturbations of $(\sigma,\alpha)$.

Fix a set $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$ compactly contained in the visible set $\mathcal{M}$
If $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$
Let $\alpha^{0}$ be as above related to some fixed $\sigma_{0}$. Assume that $I_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$

nodes.name: $f$ is compactly supported inside $\Omega$
nodes.statement: We will need to assume that $f$ is compactly supported within $\Omega$, which in particular will allow us to treat the reflected ray as a smooth regular curve in the sense of \cite{xraygeneric} since the integrand vanishes near the points of reflection. By using the path unfolding approach, we can relatively easily obtain the following microlocal result.
