Continuing in this way, we obtain a space consisting of $N+1$ copies of $\Omega$, each reflected along a specific edge. If $\gamma_{0}$ contains a corner point, we can add additional reflected copies of $\Omega$ as necessary to accommodate nearby broken rays. We also obtain a distribution $\widetilde{f} \in \mathcal{E}'(\widetilde{\Omega})$ and an unfolded version of $\gamma_{0}$, denoted by $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$, using the same process. Note that by reversing the reflection sequence, any covector $(\widetilde{z}, \widetilde{\xi}) \in T^{*}\widetilde{\Omega}$ corresponds to a unique covector $(z,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega$.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Reflect $\Omega$ successively across the hyperplanes at the reflection points to build $\widetilde{\Omega}$, $\widetilde{f}$ and $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$.

nodes.name: Introduce local coordinates $(\theta,t)$ along the unfolded straight line
nodes.statement: Since the edges of $\Omega$ are flat, it follows that $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$ is a straight line. The openness of $E$ and the assumptions on $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ ensure that for $(x,\theta)$ in a neighborhood $V \subset \Gamma_{-}(E)$ of $(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$, the unfolded paths $\widetilde{\gamma}_{x,\theta}$ lie in the same extended space $\widetilde{\Omega}$ and avoid $\partial E$. Now choose a point $p_{0}$ on the line $x_{0} + t\theta_{0}$ for $t < 0$ so that $p_{0} \notin \widetilde{\Omega}$. Define $x = p_{0} + t\theta$. Then $(\theta, t)$ are local coordinates near any point of $\widetilde{\Omega} \cap \widetilde{\gamma}_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$. We can assume without loss of generality that $\theta_{0} = (0,1)$. Writing $x = (x^{1},x^{2}) = (\theta^{1}, t)$, we have the coordinates \begin{equation*} U = \{x = (\theta^{1}, t) \, | \, |\theta^{1}| < \epsilon, \, l^{-} < t < l^{+} \} \subset \widetilde{\Omega}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Since the unfolded ray is straight, parametrize a neighborhood by $x = p_0 + t\theta$ with constant $l^{\pm}$.

nodes.name: Apply the generic-curve argument to the unfolded covector
nodes.statement: Since $f$ is compactly supported inside of $\Omega$, we may shrink $\epsilon$ as necessary so that we can take $l^{-}, l^{+}$ to be constant. Now as in the proof of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric}, we let $(z_{0}, \xi_{0} )\in N^{*}\gamma_{0}$. Then consider the corresponding reflected covector via path unfolding given by $(\widetilde{z}^{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \in N^{*}\widetilde{\gamma}_{0}$. That is, let $\{\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\ldots, \xi_{m}\}$ the sequence of normal vectors corresponding to the ordered reflection points of the path $\gamma_{0}$ up until reaching the point $z_{0}$. Let $R_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ be the reflection operators across each affine hyperplane $z \cdot \xi_{j} = x_{0,j} \cdot \xi_{j}$ for $1 \leq j \leq m$. Specifically, $R_{j}v = v- 2((v-x_{0,j})\cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{z}_{0} = Rz_{0} := R_{1}R_{2} \cdots R_{m}z_{0}$. Also, consider the operators $A_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ defined as reflections across the hyperplanes $z \cdot \xi_{j} = 0$ that pass through the origin. Specifically, $A_{j}v = v - 2(v \cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{\xi}_{0} = A\xi_{0} := A_{1}A_{2} \cdots A_{m_{z_{0}}}\xi_{0}$. The argument of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric} shows that $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(\widetilde{f})$.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Map $(z_0,\xi_0)$ to $(\widetilde{z}_0,\widetilde{\xi}_0)$ by the reflection operators $R_j, A_j$ and invoke Proposition 1 of the cited work.

nodes.name: Undo the reflections to conclude
nodes.statement:
Now we undo the reflection process to conclude that $(z_{0}, \xi_{0}) 
otin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$. In particular, we use the respective inverse transformations $A^{-1}$ and $R^{-1}$, generated by $A_{j}^{-1} = A_{j}$ and $R_{j}^{-1} = R_{j}$ to recover $(z_{0},\xi_{0})$ from $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0})$. Note that the reflections $A_{j}, R_{j}$ preserve the singularities of $f$, and so the analytic wavefront set of $\widetilde{f}$ transforms in the obvious way. Thus $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) = (Rz_{0}, A\xi_{0}) 
otin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(\widetilde{f}) \Longrightarrow (z_{0}, \xi_{0}) 
otin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: The involutions $A_j, R_j$ preserve singularities, so the conclusion transfers back to $(z_0,\xi_0)$ and $f$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Suppose $I_{\sigma, E}f = 0$. By Proposition \ref{thm:microlocalsquare} we have that $f$ is analytic on $K$. Since $\mathrm{supp}(f) \subset K$, we have that $f$ can be extended to an entire function and hence must be identically zero.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 makes $f$ analytic on $K$; a compactly supported entire extension must vanish.

nodes.name: Deduce analyticity from the microlocal proposition
nodes.statement: Suppose $I_{\sigma, E}f = 0$. By Proposition \ref{thm:microlocalsquare} we have that $f$ is analytic on $K$.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing data plus Proposition 1 gives $f$ analytic on $K$.

nodes.name: Conclude $f \equiv 0$ by entire extension
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{supp}(f) \subset K$, we have that $f$ can be extended to an entire function and hence must be identically zero.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: A compactly supported entire function vanishes identically.

nodes.name: Two adjacent edges suffice, two opposite edges fail
nodes.statement: In the case of the square Theorem \ref{thm:injectivesquare} gives injectivity on the whole domain if $E$ contains two adjacent (closed) edges. However, one must be careful since it fails for $E$ consisting of two opposite edges.
nodes.section: Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square

nodes.name: $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$ is fixed
nodes.statement: We will always suppose that $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$ is fixed, where $\mathcal{M} \subset \Omega$ is the visible set.

nodes.name: Proposition 2 (decomposition of the normal operator)
nodes.statement: $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic} + N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}$ where $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$, elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$, and $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha,reflect}$ is an operator with $C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega \times \Omega)$ Schwartz kernel. Thus there exists a classical pseudo differential operator $Q$ in $\Omega$ of order $1$ such that \begin{equation} QN_{\sigma, E,\alpha}f = f + QN_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}f + S_{1} \end{equation} for any $f \in \mathcal{D}'(K)$, where $S_{1}$ is an operator with $C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega \times \Omega)$ Schwartz kernel.
nodes.statement_short: $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ splits into an elliptic order $-1$ $\Psi$DO (ballistic) plus a smoothing operator, giving a parametrix identity $QN f = f + QN_{reflect}f + S_1$.
assumptions: for any $f \in \mathcal{D}'(K)$
conclusions: $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic} + N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}$ where $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$, elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$, and $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha,reflect}$ is an operator with $C_{0}^{\infty}(\Omega \times \Omega)$ Schwartz kernel
QN_{\sigma, E,\alpha}f = f + QN_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}f + S_{1}

nodes.name: Domain assumed open with piecewise smooth convex boundary
nodes.statement: For now, we will only assume that the domain $\Omega$ is an open subset of $\rn{n}$ with piecewise smooth, convex boundary. In \S \ref{sec:normalsimplify} and beyond we then work specifically with the square $(0,1) \times (0,1)$.

nodes.name: Cutoff chosen so the number of reflections is constant on its support
nodes.statement: Choose a cutoff function $\alpha(x,\theta)$ on $\Gamma_{-}$ such that $\alpha I_{\sigma, E}$ has a constant number of reflections $N \geq 0$ on its support.

nodes.name: Adjoint computation for $\alpha I_{\sigma,E}$
nodes.statement: The adjoint to $\alpha I_{\sigma,E}$ can be computed as follows: \begin{align} & \quad \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\alpha(x,\theta) [I_{\sigma,E}f](x,\theta) g(x,\theta)\,d\Sigma \\ & = \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\alpha(x,\theta) g(x,\theta) \sum_{j=0}^{N}\int_{\rn{+}} w_{j}(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})f(z_{j} + t \theta_{j})|\nu(x) \cdot \theta|\,dt\,dS(x)\,d\theta \notag \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Pairing $\alpha I_{\sigma,E}f$ with $g$ in $L^2(\Gamma_-,d\Sigma)$ written out as a sum of segment integrals.

nodes.name: Change of variables $(x,\theta,t) \mapsto (y,\eta)$
nodes.statement:
For each $j$ we make the change of variables $(x,	heta,t) \mapsto (y,\eta)$ where $(y,\eta) := (z_{j}(x,	heta)+t	heta_{j}(x,	heta), 	heta_{j}(x,	heta))$. Thus  egin{align} (x,	heta) & = (z_{-j}(y,\eta), 	heta_{-j}(y,\eta))
otag\ t & = -	au_{-}(y,\eta). \end{align} Intuitively, in moving from $(y,\eta)$ to $\left( z_{-j}(y,\eta), 	heta_{-j}(y,\eta) ight)$, we first project from the point $y$ to the boundary along the direction $-\eta$ and then trace backwards along the trajectory for the previous $j$ reflections. We compute  egin{align} & \Big(z_{m}(x,	heta) + s	heta_{m}(x,	heta), 	heta_{m}(x,	heta)\Big)
otag\ & = \left(z_{m}\Big(z_{-j}(y,\eta), 	heta_{-j}(y,\eta)\Big) + s	heta_{m}\Big(z_{-j}(y,\eta), 	heta_{-j}(y,\eta)\Big), 	heta_{m}\Big(z_{-j}(y,\eta), 	heta_{-j}(y,\eta)\Big)ight)
otag\ & = (z_{m-j}(y,\eta)+s	heta_{m-j}(y,\eta), \, 	heta_{m-j}(y,\eta)).
otag \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $(y,\eta) = (z_j + t\theta_j, \theta_j)$ inverts to $(x,\theta) = (z_{-j}(y,\eta),\theta_{-j}(y,\eta))$, $t = -\tau_-(y,\eta)$, and composes to shift indices by $-j$.

nodes.name: Transformed integral and the Jacobian factor $J_{j}$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} & \sum_{j=0}^{N}\int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\alpha(z_{-j}(y,\eta), \theta_{-j}(y,\eta))g(z_{-j}(y,\eta), \theta_{-j}(y,\eta))w_{j}(y,\eta)f(y) J_{j}(y,\eta)\,dy\,d\eta, \end{align*} where \begin{equation*} J_{j}(y,\eta) = \left| \frac{\partial x \partial \theta \partial t}{\partial y \, \partial \eta}\right| |\nu(z_{-j}(y,\eta))\cdot \theta_{-j}(y,\eta)|. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The adjoint pairing becomes an integral over $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ with Jacobian factor $J_j(y,\eta)$.

nodes.name: $J_{j}(y,\eta) = 1$ by invariance of the symplectic form under the billiard map
nodes.statement: Since the billiard map $T$ preserves the symplectic form $|\nu(x) \cdot \theta| dx \wedge d\theta$ on $\Gamma_{-}$, it follows that $J_{j}(y,\eta) = 1$. We stress that this is even true for domains with piecewise smooth boundary as is the case for the square, by measure theoretic arguments (see \cite{serge2} \S 1.7).
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of $|\nu \cdot \theta| dx \wedge d\theta$ under $T$ makes the Jacobian equal to one, even for piecewise smooth boundary.
assumptions: Since the billiard map $T$ preserves the symplectic form $|\nu(x) \cdot \theta| dx \wedge d\theta$ on $\Gamma_{-}$
conclusions: it follows that $J_{j}(y,\eta) = 1$
this is even true for domains with piecewise smooth boundary as is the case for the square, by measure theoretic arguments

nodes.name: Adjoint formula for $(\alpha I_{\sigma,E})^{*}$
nodes.statement: Thus we have \begin{align} (\alpha I_{\sigma, E})^{*}g(x) & = \sum_{j=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}[\alpha g](z_{-j}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j}(x,\theta)) w_{j}(x,\theta) \,d\theta \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $(\alpha I_{\sigma,E})^*g(x)$ is a sum over $j$ of sphere integrals of $[\alpha g](z_{-j},\theta_{-j})w_j$.

nodes.name: Normal operator $I^{*}_{\sigma,E}I_{\sigma,E}$ split into reflected and ballistic parts
nodes.statement:
We are now ready to compute the normal operator $I_{\sigma,E}^{*}I_{\sigma,E}$. By definition  egin{align} & I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}^{*}I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}f(x) 
otag\ & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}|\alpha(z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))|^{2}I_{\sigma,E}f(z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta)\, d	heta
otag\ & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{N} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|\alpha(z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))|^{2} \, w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta)
otag\ & \quad \cdot w_{j_{2}}(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta)+t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta)) \, f\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) + t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta)ight)\,dt\,d	heta 
otag\ & =\sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2} 
eq j_{1}}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta)\,w_{j_{2}}(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) + t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta)) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot |\alpha(z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))|^{2}\, f\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) + t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) ight)\,dt\,d	heta
otag\ & + \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\, w_{j_{1}}(x+t	heta,	heta)w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta) \, |\alpha(z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))|^{2} \, f\left(x +	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta + t	heta ight)\,dt\,d	heta 
otag\ & =: N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f(x) + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $I^*I$ and separating $j_1 = j_2$ yields $N_{reflect} + N_{ballistic}$.

nodes.name: Full normal operator for the partition $\{\alpha_{k}\}$ and its ballistic/reflected parts
nodes.statement: It follows that the full normal operator $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$, corresponding to the partition by smooth cutoff functions $\alpha_{k}$, is given by the sum \begin{align*} & N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}f(x) \\ & = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N_k}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} |\alpha_{k}(z_{-j_{1}}, \theta_{-j_{1}})|^{2} w_{j_{1}}\left( x,\theta \right) w_{j_{2}}\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}+ t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}, \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}\right)\\ & \cdot f\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}+ t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}\right)\, dt\,d\theta \end{align*} We pick off the ballistic terms where $j_{1}=j_{2}$ to decompose $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}f$ as a sum \begin{equation*} N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma,E,\alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect} \end{equation*} with \begin{align*} & N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}f(x)\\ & = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\sum_{j=0}^{N_{k}}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} |\alpha_{k}(z_{-j}, \theta_{-j})|^{2} w_{j}\left( x,\theta \right) w_{j}\left(x + (\tau_{-}(x,\theta)+t)\theta, \theta\right)\\ & \qquad \cdot f\left(x + (\tau_{-}(x,\theta)+t)\theta \right)\, dt\,d\theta\\ & = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\sum_{j=0}^{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}} |\alpha_{k}(z_{-j}, \theta_{-j})|^{2} w_{j}\left( x,\theta \right) w_{j}\left(x + t\theta, \theta\right)f\left(x + t\theta \right)\, dt\,d\theta\\ & = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\sum_{j=0}^{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\rn{+}} \left[ |\alpha_{k}(z_{-j}(x,\cdot) \theta_{-j}(x,\cdot))(\theta)|^{2} w_{j}\left( x,\cdot \right) w_{j}\left(x + t\theta, \cdot \right)\right]_{even}(\theta)\\ & \qquad \cdot f\left(x + t\theta \right)\, dt\,d\theta \end{align*} and \begin{align*} N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}f(x) & = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N_{k}}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2} \neq j_{1}}^{N_k}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} |\alpha_{k}(z_{-j_{1}}, \theta_{-j_{1}})|^{2}\\ & \cdot w_{j_{1}}\left( x,\theta \right) w_{j_{2}}\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}+ t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}, \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}\right)f\left(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}+ t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}\right)\, dt\,d\theta. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit double-sum integral formulas for $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$, $N_{ballistic}$ (with even part in $\theta$) and $N_{reflect}$.

nodes.name: Even part of a function in the direction variable
nodes.statement: The notation $\left[ g(x,\cdot) \right]_{even}(\theta)$ is the even part of $g$ in the variable $\theta$, defined by $\left[ g(x,\cdot)\right]_{even}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\left[ g(x,\theta) + g(x,-\theta) \right]$.
nodes.genus: the even part of $g$ in the variable $\theta$

nodes.name: $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}$ is an elliptic classical $\Psi$DO of order $-1$
nodes.statement: By Lemma 2 of \cite{xraygeneric} $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha, ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$ with principal symbol \begin{equation} a_{0}(x,\xi) = 2\pi \sum_{k=0}^{K}\sum_{j=0}^{N_{k}}\int_{\theta \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, \, \theta \cdot \xi = 0}|\alpha_{k}(z_{-j}, \theta_{-j})|^{2} \left| w_{j}\left( x,\theta \right)\right|^2 \,d\theta \end{equation} The bound on the number of reflections $N_{max}$ ensures that the integral kernel has a positive lower bound on the set of all covectors $(x,\xi)$ such that it is non vanishing at some $\theta \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ normal to $\xi$. Clearly, $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}$ is also elliptic on the set $\mathcal{M}'$.
nodes.statement_short: By the cited lemma the ballistic part is a classical $\Psi$DO of order $-1$ with principal symbol $a_0$, elliptic on $\mathcal{M}'$.
assumptions: The bound on the number of reflections $N_{max}$ ensures that the integral kernel has a positive lower bound on the set of all covectors $(x,\xi)$ such that it is non vanishing at some $\theta \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ normal to $\xi$
conclusions: $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha, ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$ with principal symbol
$N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,ballistic}$ is also elliptic on the set $\mathcal{M}'$

nodes.name: Strategy for the reflected part of the normal operator
nodes.statement: For the reflected part of the normal operator, our goal will be to make a change of variables so that $f(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}} + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}})$ becomes $f(y)$, with the hope that what we obtain is either a weakly singular integral operator (i.e. smoothing of order $-1$) or an operator with $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernel. It turns out that the latter will hold. This technique is very much inspired by the kind of substitution used in \cite{inversesource, hubenthal}, and also in \cite{xraygeneric} for the non-Euclidean case. For now, we will still be working with the part of the operator that avoids broken rays with corner points.
nodes.statement_short: Change variables so that the argument of $f$ becomes $y$, aiming for (and obtaining) a $C_0^\infty$ Schwartz kernel.

nodes.name: Unfolded coordinates $\widetilde{z}$ of the reflection point
nodes.statement: Let $(x,\theta) \in \Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$, suppose we have some smooth cutoff $\alpha$ on $\Gamma_{-}(E)$. By construction, all broken rays originating from the support of $\alpha$ have the same sequence of reflection signatures. Let $\{(h_{1},v_{1}), \ldots, (h_{N},v_{N})\}$ be the ordered set of all such pairs (see Figure \ref{fig:beam}). Let $z = z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta)$ (i.e. $z$ is the $j_{2}^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection point on $\partial \Omega$ of the broken ray starting at $(z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))$). Then $(h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})$ is the reflection signature from $x$ to $z$, and so we consider \begin{equation*} \widetilde{z} := R_{h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}}}(z) = (\widetilde{z}^{1}, \widetilde{z}^{2}) \end{equation*} as the associated unfolded coordinates of $z$. Up to a rotation of $\Omega$, there are essentially two possibilities depending on whether $\widetilde{z}$ lies on a top or right edge of a reflected copy of the square. We will use $\theta$ to denote an angle value in radians and $\widehat{\theta} = (\cos{\theta}, \sin{\theta})$ to denote its associated direction vector. Furthermore, if $x \in \rn{2}$, we define $x^{\perp} = (-x^{2},x^{1})$. For simplicity of notation, we let $(l_{1},l_{2}) = (h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})$.
nodes.statement_short: With $z = z_{j_2-j_1}(x,\theta)$, set $\widetilde{z} = R_{h_{j_2}-h_{j_1}, v_{j_2}-v_{j_1}}(z)$ and write $(l_1,l_2)$ for that signature.
differentia: $(h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})$ is the reflection signature from $x$ to $z$

nodes.name: Unfolded reflection point $\widetilde{z}$ as a function of $x$ and $\theta$
nodes.statement: We have one of the following equations for $\widetilde{z}$ as a function of the starting point $x$ with direction $\theta$: \begin{align} \widetilde{z} & = (\widetilde{z}^{1}, l_{2}) = (x^{1} + (l_{2} - x^{2})\cot{\theta}, l_{2})\\ \widetilde{z} & = (l_{1}, \widetilde{z}^{2}) = (l_{1}, x^{2} + (l_{1} - x^{1})\tan{\theta}). \end{align}

nodes.name: Reflection point $z(x,\eta)$ after the substitution $\eta = S_{l_1,l_2}(\theta)$
nodes.statement: In the integral expression of the normal operator, we first make the substitution $\eta = S_{l_{1},l_{2}}(\theta)$, which is the reflected angle after applying the billiard map $j_{2}-j_{1}$ times to $(x+\tau_{-}(x,\widehat{\theta})\widehat{\theta},\, \widehat{\theta})$. Note that $|l_{1}|+|l_{2}| = j_{2} - j_{1}$. Obviously, the Jacobian determinant of this transformation is $1$. We also rewrite $z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\widehat{\theta}) = \pi_{1} \circ T^{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x+\tau_{-}(x,\widehat{\theta})\widehat{\theta}, \widehat{\theta})$ as the function $z(x,\eta)$. In particular, we may have either \begin{align} z(x,\eta) & = R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}\left(x^{1} + (l_{2} - x^{2})\cot\left(S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\eta)\right),\quad l_{2}\right)\\ & = \left((-1)^{l_{1}+1}l_{1} + \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{1}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{1}}\left[ x^{1} + (l_{2} - x^{2})\cot\left(S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\eta)\right) \right], \quad \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{2}}}{2} \right) \notag \end{align} or \begin{align} z(x,\eta) & = R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}\left(l_{1}, \quad x^{2} + (l_{1} - x^{1})\tan\left(S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\eta)\right) \right) \\ & = \left(\frac{1-(-1)^{l_{1}}}{2}, \quad (-1)^{l_{2}+1}l_{2} + \frac{1-(-1)^{l_{2}}}{2} + (-1)^{l_{2}}\left[ x^{2} + (l_{1} - x^{1})\tan\left(S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\eta)\right) \right] \right).\notag \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Rewriting $z_{j_2-j_1}$ in terms of the unfolded angle $\eta$, with unit Jacobian.

nodes.name: Jacobian determinant of the substitution $y = z(x,\eta) + t\widehat{\eta}$
nodes.statement: Thus we have an integrand involving $f(z(x,\eta) + t\widehat{\eta})$, where $\widehat{\eta} = (\cos{\eta},\sin{\eta})$. The next step is to make the substitution $y = z(x,\eta) + t\widehat{\eta}$ (see Figure \ref{fig:substitution}). We compute it's Jacobian determinant to be \begin{align} \left| \frac{\partial y}{\partial \eta \partial t} \right| & = |(-1)^{l_{2}}(l_{2}-x^{2})\csc{\eta} + t| = |(l_{2}-x^{2})\csc{\theta} + t| = |\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{z}|\left| \frac{l_{2}-x^{2}}{\widetilde{y}^{2} - \widetilde{z}^{2}} + 1 \right|\notag\\ & = |\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{z}|\left| \frac{\widetilde{y}^{2}-x^{2}}{\widetilde{y}^{2} - l_{2}} \right| \end{align} if $z(x,\eta)$ is given by (\ref{eq:zxeta1}). Similarly, we obtain \begin{equation*} \left| \frac{\partial y}{\partial \eta \partial t} \right| = |(-1)^{l_{1}}(l_{1} -x^{1})\sec{\eta} + t | = |\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{z}|\left| \frac{\widetilde{y}^{1}-x^{1}}{\widetilde{y}^{1} - l_{1}} \right| \end{equation*} when $z(x,\eta)$ is given by (\ref{eq:zxeta2}). Here we've used the fact that $\sec{\eta} = (-1)^{l_{1}}\sec{\theta}$ and $\csc{\eta} = (-1)^{l_{2}} \csc{\theta}$.
nodes.statement_short: $|\partial y / \partial \eta \partial t| = |\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{z}||(\widetilde{y}^i - x^i)/(\widetilde{y}^i - l_i)|$ in each of the two edge cases.

nodes.name: Auxiliary reflection-law equations expressing $\widetilde{z}$ via $x$ and $y$
nodes.statement: In order to fully carry out the substitution in the integral, we need to write $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$. We will need the auxiliary equation \begin{equation} (\widetilde{y} - \widetilde{z}) \cdot (\widetilde{z} - x)^{\perp} = 0, \end{equation} which is a consequence of the reflection law. In the case where $\widetilde{z}^{2}$ is undetermined, we have $\widetilde{z}^{1} = l_{1}$ and then \begin{equation} \widetilde{z}^{2} - \widetilde{y}^{2} = \frac{(\widetilde{y}^{2}-x^{2})(l_{1} - \widetilde{y}^{1})}{\widetilde{y}^{1} - x^{1}}. \end{equation} Similarly, if $\widetilde{z}^{1}$ is undetermined then \begin{equation} \widetilde{z}^{1} - \widetilde{y}^{1} = \frac{(\widetilde{y}^{1} - x^{1})(l_{2} - \widetilde{y}^{2})}{\widetilde{y}^{2} - x^{2}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The orthogonality relation $(\widetilde{y}-\widetilde{z})\cdot(\widetilde{z}-x)^{\perp} = 0$ and the resulting formulas for the undetermined component of $\widetilde{z}$.

nodes.name: The Jacobian simplifies to $|\widetilde{y}-x|$ and stays bounded away from zero
nodes.statement_short: The Jacobian equals $|\widetilde{y}-x|$, which is bounded below by $d(\mathrm{supp}(f),\partial\Omega)$ whenever $(l_1,l_2) \neq (0,0)$, so $1/|\widetilde{y}-x|$ is smooth.
assumptions: so long as $l_{1}$ or $l_{2}$ is nonzero (i.e. $j_{2} - j_{1} \neq 0$)
conclusions: = |\widetilde{y} - x|.
$|\widetilde{y}-x|$ is strictly positive for all $x,y \in \mathrm{supp}(f)$
the reciprocal factor $\frac{1}{|\widetilde{y}-x|}$ resulting from the change of variables is smooth and bounded as a function of $y$ and $x$

nodes.name: Unfolded direction $\widehat{\eta}$ in terms of $\widetilde{y}-x$
nodes.statement: Using again the fact that $\cos{\eta} = (-1)^{l_{1}}\cos{\theta}$, $\sin{\eta} = (-1)^{l_{2}}\sin{\theta}$ we have that \begin{equation*} \widehat{\eta} = ((-1)^{l_{1}}\cos{\theta},(-1)^{l_{2}}\sin{\theta}) = \frac{1}{|\widetilde{y}-x|}( (-1)^{l_{1}}(\widetilde{y}^{1}- x^{1}), (-1)^{l_{2}}(\widetilde{y}^{2} - x^{2})). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Terms comprising $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha,reflect}$ after the substitution
nodes.statement: Altogether, we obtain that $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha, reflect}f(x)$ consists of a sum of terms of the form \begin{equation} \int_{\rn{2}} |\alpha_{k}(T^{-j_{2}}(y + \tau_{-}(y,\widehat{\eta})\widehat{\eta}, \widehat{\eta}))|^{2} w_{j_{1}}\left( x,\frac{\widetilde{y}-x}{|\widetilde{y}-x|} \right) w_{j_{2}}\left(y, \widehat{\eta}\right)f\left(y\right)\, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y} -x|}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Each reflected term becomes an integral over $\rn{2}$ against $f(y)\,dy/|\widetilde{y}-x|$.

nodes.name: Care needed for smoothness when a ray starts at a corner
nodes.statement: Note that one must be very careful in the above formulation in order to show that the integrand in (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) is smooth where it is supported. Consider the case if $\alpha_{k}$ is non vanishing for a broken ray which starts at a corner point, but still none of the broken rays in the support of $\alpha$ contain another corner point after some positive number of reflections. Within the factor of (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) given by \begin{equation*} |\alpha_{k}(T^{-j_{2}}(y + \tau_{-}(y,\widehat{\eta})\widehat{\eta}, \widehat{\eta}))|^{2}, \end{equation*} we see that $T^{-j_{2}}(y + \tau_{-}(y,\widehat{\eta})\widehat{\eta}, \widehat{\eta})$ fails to be smooth for $(y, \eta)$ that are pulled back to this corner point. However, as previously discussed, the construction of $\alpha_{k}$ ensures that it is smooth on $\rn{2}\times \mathbb{S}^{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $T^{-j_2}$ is non-smooth at pullbacks of a corner starting point, but $\alpha_k$ was constructed to be smooth on $\rn{2}\times\mathbb{S}^1$.

nodes.name: Rotate so that all $h_{j}, v_{j}$ are nonnegative and nondecreasing
nodes.statement: By a possible rotation of $\Omega$, we may as well assume that $h_{j},v_{j}$ are all nonnegative. Clearly each sequence $\{h_{j}\}$, $\{v_{j}\}$ is also nondecreasing in this case.

nodes.name: Backward boundary points $q_{j}(y,\eta)$ on the circumscribed circle
nodes.statement: Next define the function $q_{j}(y, \eta)$ for $1 \leq j \leq N$ as the \textit{final} intersection point of the line $R_{h_{j},v_{j}}(y) + t \widehat{S_{h_{j},v_{j}}^{-1}(\eta)}$ with $\partial B$ for $t \leq 0$. We also define $q_{0}(y,\eta) = y + \tau_{-,\partial B}(y,\eta) \widehat{\eta}$ where $\tau_{-,\partial B}(y,\widehat{\eta})$ is the negative distance to $\partial B$ from $y$ in the direction $-\widehat{\eta}$, defined for $(y,\widehat{\eta}) \in B \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $q_j$ is the last backward intersection with $\partial B$ of the unfolded line, and $q_0$ the backward $\partial B$ endpoint from $y$.
nodes.genus: the \textit{final} intersection point of the line $R_{h_{j},v_{j}}(y) + t \widehat{S_{h_{j},v_{j}}^{-1}(\eta)}$ with $\partial B$

nodes.name: Smooth replacement of the cutoff factor by $\alpha_{k}(q_{j_2}, \widehat{S^{-1}})$
nodes.statement: We can then replace $\alpha_{k}(T^{-j_{2}}(y + \tau_{-}(y,\widehat{\eta})\widehat{\eta}, \widehat{\eta}))$ with \begin{equation} \alpha_{k}(q_{j_{2}}(y,\widehat{\eta}), \, \widehat{S_{h_{j_{2}}, v_{j_{2}}}^{-1}(\eta)}). \end{equation} Clearly, (\ref{eq:smoothalphakterm}) depends smoothly on $y, \eta$.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $T^{-j_2}$ by the circumscribed-circle map $q_{j_2}$ makes the cutoff factor depend smoothly on $(y,\eta)$.

nodes.name: The reflected term is a smoothing integral operator
nodes.statement: We observe that the definitions of $w_{j_{1}}, w_{j_{2}}$ also involve $\tau_{-}$, which is not smooth on $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$. However, since $\sigma$ is compactly supported inside of $\Omega$ on some smooth subdomain, we can modify $\tau_{-}$ inside of $w_{j_{1}},w_{j_{2}}$ as necessary to be smooth without changing the integrals. In particular, we can use the functions $q_{j}$ to define the weight functions instead of the billiard map $T$ and boundary distance function $\tau_{-}$. Therefore, (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) is a smoothing integral operator.
nodes.statement_short: Replacing $\tau_-$ and $T$ by the smooth functions $q_j$ inside the weights leaves the integrals unchanged and makes the reflected term smoothing.
assumptions: since $\sigma$ is compactly supported inside of $\Omega$ on some smooth subdomain
conclusions: we can modify $\tau_{-}$ inside of $w_{j_{1}},w_{j_{2}}$ as necessary to be smooth without changing the integrals
(\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) is a smoothing integral operator

nodes.name: Why broken rays with corners must be kept in the normal operator
nodes.statement: Recall from the proof of Proposition \ref{thm:microlocalsquare} that by unfolding the broken rays, corner points posed no problem. This meant we didn't have to remove any covectors from $\mathcal{M}'$ whose corresponding broken rays passed through a corner point. It is thus important to also consider broken rays with corners for the normal operator so as to make $\mathcal{M}'$ as big as possible. However, for this we no longer have the option of path unfolding, so it will be necessary to treat reflections more directly.
nodes.statement_short: Unfolding tolerated corners in Proposition 1, so keeping corner rays makes $\mathcal{M}'$ as large as possible, but reflections must now be handled directly.

nodes.name: Broken ray through a corner as a limit of corner-avoiding broken rays
nodes.statement: While the corners of $\partial \Omega$ have no well-defined normal vector, we can make sense of a broken ray that touches a corner point by realizing it as a limit of broken rays that avoid the corner. This is described in detail in the 2-dimensional case in the work of Eskin in \cite{eskin}. Essentially, in 2-dimensions there are two reflection directions at a corner point that can be obtained as a limit of broken rays starting at some fixed point $x \in \Omega$ and with reflection point approaching the given corner. In higher dimensions, one can obtain a cone of possible reflection directions, which is thus a hypersurface. However, for the square (or even the $n$-cube), these limiting rays all conveniently coincide.
nodes.statement_short: A corner-touching broken ray is defined as a limit of rays avoiding the corner; in 2D there are two limiting directions, which coincide for the square.
nodes.definiendum: a broken ray that touches a corner point
nodes.genus: limit of broken rays that avoid the corner
differentia: in 2-dimensions there are two reflection directions at a corner point that can be obtained as a limit of broken rays starting at some fixed point $x \in \Omega$ and with reflection point approaching the given corner
for the square (or even the $n$-cube), these limiting rays all conveniently coincide

nodes.name: At a corner of the square the broken ray reflects straight back
nodes.statement: To see this, let $x\in \Omega$ and let $c$ be a corner point. Define $\theta_{c}$ as the angle between $c-x$ and the horizontal axis. For $\theta$ close to $\theta_{c}$, the broken ray from $x$ in the direction $\widehat{\theta}$ will intersect twice near $c$ and return at an angle $\pi+\theta$ with the positive horizontal direction (i.e. it will return in the direction $-\widehat{\theta}$). Therefore, the limit of such rays shows that $\gamma_{x,\theta_{c}}$ unambiguously reflects back towards $x$. This is also consistent with what one expects from path unfolding.
nodes.statement_short: Rays with direction near $\theta_c$ return in direction $-\widehat{\theta}$, so $\gamma_{x,\theta_c}$ unambiguously reflects back towards $x$.
assumptions: let $x\in \Omega$ and let $c$ be a corner point
For $\theta$ close to $\theta_{c}$
conclusions: the broken ray from $x$ in the direction $\widehat{\theta}$ will intersect twice near $c$ and return at an angle $\pi+\theta$ with the positive horizontal direction
the limit of such rays shows that $\gamma_{x,\theta_{c}}$ unambiguously reflects back towards $x$

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (a regular broken ray has at most two corner points)
nodes.statement: A regular broken ray starting from $E$ contains at most two corner points, and if it has two, then the first one is its starting point.
assumptions: A regular broken ray starting from $E$
conclusions: contains at most two corner points, and if it has two, then the first one is its starting point

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with two distinct corner points. Since reflections from corners return in the opposite direction from the direction of incidence, any broken ray between them will repeat periodically. Thus, either one of the corner points lies in $E$, or there is a point along the broken ray between them that lies in $E$. But this implies the broken ray would have terminated before hitting both corners.
nodes.statement_short: If two corners occurred, the corner-to-corner segment would repeat periodically, so the ray must already have terminated on $E$ -- contradiction.

nodes.name: Assume two corner points and observe periodicity
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with two distinct corner points. Since reflections from corners return in the opposite direction from the direction of incidence, any broken ray between them will repeat periodically.
nodes.statement_short: Corner reflections reverse direction, so a path between two corners repeats periodically.

nodes.name: Derive the contradiction with termination on $E$
nodes.statement: Thus, either one of the corner points lies in $E$, or there is a point along the broken ray between them that lies in $E$. But this implies the broken ray would have terminated before hitting both corners.
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity forces a point of the ray to lie in $E$, so it would have terminated before both corners.

nodes.name: Notation and support conventions for the corner analysis
nodes.statement: We will use $c \neq x_{0}$ to refer to a corner in the broken ray if it has one, and we will allow for the possibility that $x_{0}$ itself is a corner point. However, as previously discussed, $x_{0}$ being a corner point does not present any problem with regard to the smoothness of the integrands involved in the expansion of the localized normal operator (see the discussion following (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm})). As before, let $K \Subset \Omega$ be the set on which we assume $f$ has support.
nodes.statement_short: Write $c \neq x_0$ for an interior corner of the ray, allow $x_0$ itself to be a corner, and let $K \Subset \Omega$ contain $\mathrm{supp} f$.

nodes.name: Choice of the neighborhood $U$ of a corner-crossing broken ray
nodes.statement: So given our broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$, we assume it passes through a corner point $c \neq x_{0}$ at the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection, where $1 \leq m \leq N-1$, and $N-1$ is the total number of reflections of the curve. Choose a neighborhood $U$ consisting of $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ that are sufficiently close to $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ in the following sense. At the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection, most nearby broken rays to $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ will undergo a reflection along a very short segment near the corner on which $f$ vanishes and $\sigma = 0$. In particular, such segments do not affect the weights $w_{j}$ and so we will be able to discard them. Thus, we choose $U$ small enough so that at the $m$th reflection, all nearby broken rays to $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ either pass through the corner $c$ or hit close enough to the corner so as to reflect into a short path that contributes nothing to the integral. Note that for such broken rays from $U$ passing very near to the corner $c$ (but not actually touching it), after the $(m+1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection they will be oriented in a direction opposite their respective directions during the $(m-1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ segment. We also choose $U$ small enough so as not to introduce any new corner points among the included broken rays.
nodes.statement_short: Take $U$ so small that nearby rays either hit the corner $c$ at the $m$th reflection or reflect into a negligible short segment, with no new corners.

nodes.name: Corner indicator $\mathbbm{1}_{U}$ and the associated cutoff $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Given such an open set $U$, we let $\mathbbm{1}_{U}(x,\theta)$ be a function on $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ which is constant on lines and satisfies \begin{equation} \mathbbm{1}_{U}(x,\theta) = \left\{ \begin{array}{cc} 1 & \textrm{ if $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(t), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(t)$ passes through $U$ and intersects the corner $c$,}\\ 0 & \textrm{ otherwise } \end{array}\right. \end{equation} Also let $\alpha(x,\theta)$ be a smooth cutoff function in $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ which vanishes outside the set of lines associated with $U$.
nodes.genus: a function on $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ which is constant on lines
differentia: \textrm{ if $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(t), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(t)$ passes through $U$ and intersects the corner $c$,}

nodes.name: Localized broken ray transform and its adjoint in the presence of a corner
nodes.statement: We write the localized broken ray transform as \begin{align} I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f(x,\theta) & = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \int_{\rn{+}}(1- \mathbbm{1}_{U}(x,\theta))\alpha(x,\theta)[w_{j}f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \notag\\ & + \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \int_{\rn{+}}\mathbbm{1}_{U}(x,\theta)\alpha(x,\theta)[w_{j}f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \end{align} We then have \begin{align} I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}^{*}g(x) & = \sum_{j=0}^{N} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}[(1- \mathbbm{1}_{U})\alpha g](z_{-j}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j}(\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta)\,d\theta \notag\\ & + \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}\alpha g](z_{-}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta)\,d\theta. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Split $I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ into corner-free ($1-\mathbbm{1}_U$, $N$ reflections) and corner ($\mathbbm{1}_U$, $N-1$ reflections) parts, with matching adjoint.

nodes.name: Normal operator in the presence of a corner
nodes.statement:
Finally, the normal operator is given by  egin{align} I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}^{*}I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f(x) & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) + t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta))\, dt \,d	heta 
otag\ & + \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta) + t	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta), 	heta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,	heta))\, dt \,d	heta. \end{align} Here we've used the fact that $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})^{2} = 1 - \mathbbm{1}_{U}$.
nodes.statement_short: Double sum for $I^*I$ split by the corner indicator, using $(1-\mathbbm{1}_U)^2 = 1-\mathbbm{1}_U$.

nodes.name: Ballistic part with a corner, recombined into three sums
nodes.statement:
Then break off the part with $j_{2} = j_{1}$ to obtain  egin{align*} N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) & = \sum_{j=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j}(x,	heta))w_{j}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + 	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta+ t	heta, 	heta)\, dt \,d	heta 
otag\ & + \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j}(x,	heta))w_{j}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + 	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta + t	heta, 	heta)\, dt \,d	heta.
otag. \end{align*} Now we have to be a bit careful in order to combine both summands. In the first summand, whenever $(z_{-m}(x,	heta), 	heta_{-m}(x,	heta))$ is in the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})\alpha^{2}$, we know that $x+	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta + t	heta$ is a line segment very near the corner $c$ where $f$ vanishes. Thus we can throw out the term involving $j = m$. Now for the terms with $j < m$, we may immediately combine the summands into one, thus eliminating the presence of $\mathbbm{1}_{U}$. That is, we have  egin{align} N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) & = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(z_{-j}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j}(x,	heta))w_{j}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + 	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta+ t	heta, 	heta)\, dt \,d	heta 
otag\ & + \sum_{j_{1}=m+1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j_{1}}(x,	heta))w_{j_{1}}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j_{1}}f](x + 	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta+ t	heta, 	heta)\, dt \,d	heta 
otag\ & + \sum_{j_{2}=m}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{n{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{2}}(x,	heta),	heta_{-j_{2}}(x,	heta))w_{j_{2}}(x,	heta) 
otag\ & \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](x + 	au_{-}(x,	heta)	heta + t	heta, 	heta)\, dt \,d	heta. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Discard the $j=m$ bow-tie term, merge the $j<m$ terms, and keep the remaining corner-free and corner sums separately.

nodes.name: Matching reflection signatures across the corner and smoothness of $q_{m}$
nodes.statement: For the second and third terms of (\ref{eq:normalballistic2}), we use the fact that for each $j_{2}$ with $m \leq j_{2} \leq N-1$, $x+(\tau_{-}(x,\theta)+t)\theta$ in the third term has the same reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$ as in the second term, but with $j_{1} = j_{2} + 1$. This has to do with the supports of the corresponding cutoff functions. Fix $j_{1},j_{2}$ such that $m \leq j_{2} = j_{1}-1$, and let $(l_{1},l_{2})$ be the reflection signature of $(x,\theta)$ relative to $(z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))$ in the second term or $(z_{-j_{2}}(x,\theta), \theta_{-j_{2}}(x,\theta))$ in the third. The key idea is that both reflection signatures will be the same. Recall the circumscribed disk $B((\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$. Similar to the case with no corner point, we consider the sequence of reflection signatures $\{(h_{1},v_{1}), (h_{2},v_{2}), \ldots, (h_{N-1}, v_{N-1}) \}$ in the unfolded domain where all of the unfolded broken rays from $U$ touch and over which $f$ has nonzero integral. Thus we've cut out the tiny ``bow-tie" region near the corner $c$, which is why there are only $N-1$ such pairs. Also recall for $0 \leq m \leq N-1$ the functions $q_{m}(x,\theta)$ as the \textit{final} intersection point of the line $R_{h_{m},v_{m}}(x) + tS_{h_{m},v_{m}}^{-1}(\theta)$ with $\partial B$ for $t \leq 0$. Clearly, $q_{m}$ is smooth on the set of $(x,\theta)$ for which the integrand doesn't vanish, since $\partial B$ is smooth (see Figure \ref{fig:qm}).
nodes.statement_short: For $j_2 = j_1-1 \ge m$ the two terms share the same reflection signature, and the corresponding $q_m$ are smooth where the integrand does not vanish.

nodes.name: Regularized weight $w_{reg,j}$
nodes.statement: We then have a local regularized version of the weight function $w_{j}$ given by \begin{align} w_{reg,j}(x,\theta) & = \exp\left( -\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(x-\tau\theta, \theta)\,d\tau \right) \notag\\ & \quad \cdot \prod_{m=1}^{j}\exp\left( -\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(q_{m}(x,\theta) + \tau S_{h_{m}, v_{m}}^{-1}(\theta), S_{h_{m}, v_{m}}^{-1}(\theta))\,d\tau \right), \end{align} for $0 \leq j \leq N-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Weight built from the smooth circumscribed-circle points $q_m$ instead of the billiard map.
nodes.genus: a local regularized version of the weight function $w_{j}$

nodes.name: $w_{reg,j}$ coincides with $w_{j}$ or $w_{j-1}$ on the isolated broken rays
nodes.statement: By construction, $w_{reg,j}(x,\theta)$ coincides with $w_{j}(x,\theta)$ or $w_{j-1}(x,\theta)$ on the broken rays we've isolated, with the index depending on whether the broken ray intersects $c$.
assumptions: By construction
conclusions: $w_{reg,j}(x,\theta)$ coincides with $w_{j}(x,\theta)$ or $w_{j-1}(x,\theta)$ on the broken rays we've isolated, with the index depending on whether the broken ray intersects $c$

nodes.name: Ballistic part rewritten with the regularized weights
nodes.statement: This allows us to rewrite the ballistic part of the normal operator as \begin{align*} & N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) \\ & = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(z_{-j}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta) [w_{j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\ & + \sum_{j=m}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(q_{j}(x,\theta), S_{h_{j}, v_{j}}^{-1}(\theta))w_{reg,j}(x,\theta) [w_{reg,j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag. \end{align*} From here, we can make the change of variables $s = t + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)$. Then from Lemma 2 of \cite{xraygeneric} we have a classical pseudodifferential operator of order $-1$.
nodes.statement_short: After substituting $w_{reg,j}$ and $s = t + \tau_-$, the cited lemma yields a classical $\Psi$DO of order $-1$.

The terms with $j_{2} = m$ vanish
nodes.statement: We claim that in the first summation above, the terms with $j_{2} = m$ vanish. To see this, note that if $(x,\theta)$ is such that $z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta)$ is in the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}$, then reflecting $j_{2} = m$ times from that point will put us in the small ``bow-tie" region near $c$ on which the corresponding line integral vanishes.
nodes.statement_short: Reflecting $m$ times from the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_U)|\alpha|^2$ lands in the bow-tie region where the line integral vanishes.

nodes.statement_short: Dropping $j_2 = m$ leaves sums in which the reflection signature is constant on the support of $\alpha^2(1-\mathbbm{1}_U)$.

nodes.statement_short: After the $y$-substitution the reflected part is a double sum of integrals with kernel $|\alpha(q_{j_1},S^{-1})|^2 w_{reg,j_1}w_{reg,j_2}/|\widetilde{y}_{j_1,j_2}-x|$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: Recall that we have already shown in the discussion, see (\ref{eq:normalop}), that \begin{equation*} N_{\sigma, E, \alpha} = N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}, \end{equation*} where $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$ that is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$ (more generally on the subset of the cotangent space given by $\mathcal{M}'$). So we have a parametrix $Q$ of $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha, ballistic}$ of order $1$ that is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$. For the reflected part, we have a sum of terms of the form (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) in the case of a neighborhood of broken rays that don't have any corner points (except possibly as a starting point), or $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ has the form of (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna}), both of which have $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernels. Applying $Q$ to both sides of (\ref{eq:normalop}) yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Take a parametrix $Q$ of the elliptic ballistic part and note both reflected forms have $C_0^\infty$ Schwartz kernels.

nodes.name: Recall the ballistic/reflected decomposition
nodes.statement: Recall that we have already shown in the discussion, see (\ref{eq:normalop}), that \begin{equation*} N_{\sigma, E, \alpha} = N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}, \end{equation*} where $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is a classical pseudo differential operator of order $-1$ that is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$ (more generally on the subset of the cotangent space given by $\mathcal{M}'$).
nodes.statement_short: Restate $N = N_{ballistic} + N_{reflect}$ with $N_{ballistic}$ an elliptic $\Psi$DO of order $-1$.

nodes.name: Take a parametrix of the ballistic part
nodes.statement: So we have a parametrix $Q$ of $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha, ballistic}$ of order $1$ that is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Ellipticity on $\mathcal{M}$ gives a parametrix $Q$ of order $1$.

nodes.name: Identify the reflected part as smoothing
nodes.statement: For the reflected part, we have a sum of terms of the form (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) in the case of a neighborhood of broken rays that don't have any corner points (except possibly as a starting point), or $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ has the form of (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna}), both of which have $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernels.
nodes.statement_short: Both corner-free and corner forms of $N_{reflect}$ have $C_0^\infty$ Schwartz kernels.

nodes.name: Apply $Q$ to conclude
nodes.statement: Applying $Q$ to both sides of (\ref{eq:normalop}) yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the parametrix to conclude.

nodes.name: Proposition 3 (a priori estimate and finite dimensional kernel)
nodes.statement: Under the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:stabilityestimate}, without assuming that $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective, \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] one has the a priori estimate \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C\|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} + C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{-s}(\Omega)}, \quad \forall s; \end{equation*} \item[(b)] $\mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}}$ is finite dimensional and included in $C^{\infty}(K)$.
nodes.statement_short: Without injectivity one still gets an a priori estimate modulo $H^{-s}$, and $\mathrm{Ker}\,I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ is finite dimensional and smooth.
assumptions: Under the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:stabilityestimate}, without assuming that $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective
conclusions: \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C\|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} + C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{-s}(\Omega)}, \quad \forall s;
$\mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}}$ is finite dimensional and included in $C^{\infty}(K)$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: The proof is essentially the same as that for (\cite{xraygeneric}, Proposition 3). To prove part (a), by Proposition \ref{prop:normaldecomposition} we have that \begin{equation*} QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f = f + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f + S_{1}f =: f + S_{2}f. \end{equation*} $S_{2}$ has $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernel $S_{2}(x,y)$, and by elliptic regularity we have \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} - C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{-s}(\Omega)} \leq \|QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C \|f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \end{equation*} as desired. For part (b), if $f \in \mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha} }$, then $(\mathrm{Id} + S_{2})f = 0$, and also $S_{2}$ is a compact operator on $L^{2}(K)$ with smooth Schwartz kernel. Clearly $S_{2}f \in L^{2}$ if $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\Omega)$. Furthermore, for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we can estimate \begin{equation} \|f\|_{C^{k}(K)}= \|S_{2}f\|_{C^{k}(K)} \lesssim \mathrm{sup}_{y\in \Omega}\left( \|S_{2}(\cdot, y)\|_{C^{k}(K)} \right) \|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}. \end{equation} Therefore, $f \in C^{\infty}(\Omega)$. Finally, the fact that $I+S_{2}$ is Fredholm implies that its kernel is finite dimensional.
nodes.statement_short: Elliptic regularity applied to the parametrix identity gives (a); compactness and Fredholm theory for $\mathrm{Id}+S_2$ give (b).

nodes.name: Part (a): elliptic regularity for the parametrix identity
nodes.statement: To prove part (a), by Proposition \ref{prop:normaldecomposition} we have that \begin{equation*} QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f = f + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f + S_{1}f =: f + S_{2}f. \end{equation*} $S_{2}$ has $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernel $S_{2}(x,y)$, and by elliptic regularity we have \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} - C_{s}\|f\|_{H^{-s}(\Omega)} \leq \|QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C \|f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \end{equation*} as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Write $QNf = f + S_2f$ with $S_2$ smoothing and use elliptic regularity.

nodes.name: Part (b): compactness, smoothness and Fredholm property
nodes.statement: For part (b), if $f \in \mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha} }$, then $(\mathrm{Id} + S_{2})f = 0$, and also $S_{2}$ is a compact operator on $L^{2}(K)$ with smooth Schwartz kernel. Clearly $S_{2}f \in L^{2}$ if $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\Omega)$. Furthermore, for each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we can estimate \begin{equation} \|f\|_{C^{k}(K)}= \|S_{2}f\|_{C^{k}(K)} \lesssim \mathrm{sup}_{y\in \Omega}\left( \|S_{2}(\cdot, y)\|_{C^{k}(K)} \right) \|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}. \end{equation} Therefore, $f \in C^{\infty}(\Omega)$. Finally, the fact that $I+S_{2}$ is Fredholm implies that its kernel is finite dimensional.
nodes.statement_short: $(\mathrm{Id}+S_2)f=0$ with smooth compact $S_2$ forces $f \in C^\infty$ and a finite dimensional kernel.

nodes.name: Goal: perturb $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ in $C^{2}$
nodes.statement: Given a choice of smooth cutoff $\alpha$ and a smooth $\sigma$ vanishing near $\partial \Omega$ and such that $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective, we would like to be able to perturb $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ in $C^{2}$ slightly and still have $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha}$ be injective. We do this according to the following modified version of (\cite{xraygeneric}, Proposition 4).

nodes.name: Proposition 4 (stability of the normal operator under $C^{2}$ perturbations)
nodes.statement: Assume that $\sigma, \alpha$ are fixed and belong to $C^{2}$. Let $(\sigma', \alpha')$ be $O(\delta)$ close to $(\sigma, \alpha)$ in $C^{2}$. Then there exists a constant $C > 0$ that depends on an a priori bound on the $C^{2}$ norm of $(\sigma, \alpha)$ such that \begin{equation} \left\| (N_{\sigma', E, \alpha'} - N_{\sigma, E, \alpha})f \right\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \leq C \delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}.
nodes.statement_short: $O(\delta)$ $C^2$-perturbations of $(\sigma,\alpha)$ change the normal operator by $O(\delta)$ in the $L^2(K) \to H^1(\Omega)$ norm.
assumptions: Assume that $\sigma, \alpha$ are fixed and belong to $C^{2}$
Let $(\sigma', \alpha')$ be $O(\delta)$ close to $(\sigma, \alpha)$ in $C^{2}$
conclusions: there exists a constant $C > 0$ that depends on an a priori bound on the $C^{2}$ norm of $(\sigma, \alpha)$ such that
\left\| (N_{\sigma', E, \alpha'} - N_{\sigma, E, \alpha})f \right\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \leq C \delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4
nodes.statement: Recall that $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$, where $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is a weakly singular integral operator with smooth kernel and $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is smoothing. By the discussion in the proof of Proposition 4 of \cite{xraygeneric}, we have \begin{equation} \|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} - N_{\sigma', E, \alpha', ballistic}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \leq C \delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}. \end{equation} Similarly, the Schwartz kernels of $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ depend smoothly on $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ (see (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) and (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna})), so the same estimate holds for this term. The completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Quote the cited perturbation estimate for the weakly singular ballistic part and note the reflected kernels depend smoothly on $(\sigma,\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Perturbation estimate for the ballistic part
nodes.statement: Recall that $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$, where $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is a weakly singular integral operator with smooth kernel and $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is smoothing. By the discussion in the proof of Proposition 4 of \cite{xraygeneric}, we have \begin{equation} \|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} - N_{\sigma', E, \alpha', ballistic}\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} \leq C \delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The cited Proposition 4 argument bounds the ballistic difference by $C\delta\|f\|_{L^2(K)}$.

nodes.name: Same estimate for the reflected part
nodes.statement: Similarly, the Schwartz kernels of $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ depend smoothly on $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ (see (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) and (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna})), so the same estimate holds for this term. The completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth dependence of the reflected Schwartz kernels on $\sigma,\alpha$ gives the same bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: First note that if $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}: L^{2}(K) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})$ is injective, then $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}:L^{2}(K)\to H^{1}(\Omega)$ is also injective by an integration by parts. Next, since $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$, we may apply a parametrix $Q$ to get the equation $QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f = f + S_{1}f + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f$. Note that $S_{1} + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is compact. So by elliptic regularity we have the estimate \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C( \| N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} + \|(S_{1} + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect})f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}). \end{equation*} By Lemma 2 of \cite{stefanov1}, the compactness of the second term on the right implies that \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C'\|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}. \end{equation*} The other inequality is obvious. Finally, to prove part (b), we just use Proposition \ref{prop:normalperturb} to get \begin{align*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} & \leq C \|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f \|\\ & \leq C\|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} - C\|(N_{\sigma_{0},E,\alpha^{0}} - N_{\sigma, E, \alpha})f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}\\ & \leq C\|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} - C^{2}\delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity transfers to $N$, a parametrix plus compactness removes the lower order term, and Proposition 4 handles the $C^2$ perturbation.

nodes.name: Transfer injectivity from $I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ to $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$
nodes.statement: First note that if $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}: L^{2}(K) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})$ is injective, then $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}:L^{2}(K)\to H^{1}(\Omega)$ is also injective by an integration by parts.
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts shows $N$ is injective whenever $I$ is.

nodes.name: Apply the parametrix and elliptic regularity
nodes.statement: Next, since $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$, we may apply a parametrix $Q$ to get the equation $QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f = f + S_{1}f + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f$. Note that $S_{1} + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is compact. So by elliptic regularity we have the estimate \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C( \| N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} + \|(S_{1} + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect})f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Ellipticity on $\mathcal{M}$ yields $QNf = f + S_1f + QN_{reflect}f$ and the estimate with a compact remainder.

nodes.name: Remove the compact term
nodes.statement: By Lemma 2 of \cite{stefanov1}, the compactness of the second term on the right implies that \begin{equation*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} \leq C'\|N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}. \end{equation*} The other inequality is obvious.
nodes.statement_short: The cited lemma converts compactness of the remainder into the clean estimate; the reverse inequality is immediate.

nodes.name: Part (b) via the perturbation proposition
nodes.statement: Finally, to prove part (b), we just use Proposition \ref{prop:normalperturb} to get \begin{align*} \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)} & \leq C \|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f \|\\ & \leq C\|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} - C\|(N_{\sigma_{0},E,\alpha^{0}} - N_{\sigma, E, \alpha})f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}\\ & \leq C\|N_{\sigma_{0}, E, \alpha^{0}}f\|_{H^{1}(\Omega)} - C^{2}\delta \|f\|_{L^{2}(K)}.
nodes.statement_short: Insert Proposition 4's $O(\delta)$ bound to keep the estimate for nearby $(\sigma,\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Summary of the approach and its restrictions
nodes.statement: In this work, we have utilized the machinery of \cite{xraygeneric} for the X-ray transform with generic weights and applied it to the given broken ray transform on the Euclidean square. The technique of path unfolding can be applied to any polyhedral domain, however the square is very nice in that reflections are well-defined even at corner points. The unfolding approach also placed significant restraints on the attenuation coefficient $\sigma$, which is why we could only reasonably tackle the case $\sigma = 0$ and then use the normal operator computation to extend the results to $C_{0}^{2}$ perturbations.
nodes.statement_short: Path unfolding works for any polyhedral domain and handles the square's corners, but constrains $\sigma$, forcing the $\sigma=0$ plus perturbation route.

nodes.name: Higher dimensional polyhedra and the unit ball
nodes.statement: It is perhaps of interest to carry out similar computations for the broken ray transform on higher dimensional polyhedral domains, or domains where $\partial \Omega \setminus E$ is flat. One interesting problem to consider would be to try to get analogous microlocal results for the unit ball. However, one potential obstacle for strictly convex smooth domains is that a beam of collimated rays, upon reflection becomes uncollimated. This makes it difficult to obtain a nice integral form of the normal operator.
nodes.statement_short: Extend the analysis to higher dimensional polyhedral domains, to domains with flat $\partial\Omega \setminus E$, and to the unit ball, where reflected beams become uncollimated.
